items.text: and accessible reading interfaces—even for legacy PDFs?” We describe the Semantic Reader Project, a collaborative effort across multiple institutions to explore automatic creation of dynamic reading interfaces for research papers.
items.why: States the core goal and scope of the Semantic Reader Project.
items.plain: We present the Semantic Reader Project, a joint effort to automatically make interactive reading tools for scientific papers.

items.text: Through this project, we’ve developed ten research prototype interfaces and conducted usability studies with 300+ participants and real-world users showing improved reading experiences for scholars.
items.why: Summarizes key evaluation result and study scope across all prototypes.
items.plain: We created ten prototype interfaces and tested them with over 300 users, showing improved reading experiences for researchers.

items.text: We’ve also released a production research paper reader that will incorporate novel features as they mature.
items.why: Mentions the deployment of the production tool.
items.plain: We launched a working paper reader that will add new features as they are refined.

items.text: But when it comes to actually reading research papers, the process, based on a static PDF format, has remained largely unchanged for many decades.
items.why: Identifies the core problem with current paper reading formats.
items.plain: Reading research papers still relies on static PDF files, which have barely changed in decades.

items.text: Based on lab and field studies, CiteSee showed promise that providing visual augmentation and personalized context around inline citations in an interactive reading environment can allow readers to more effectively discover relevant prior work and keep track of their exploration during real-world literature review tasks.
items.why: Presents takeaway evaluation result for the CiteSee prototype.
items.plain: User studies showed that adding visual features and personalized context to inline citations helps readers find relevant past work and track their progress during literature reviews.

items.text: In a lab study, CiteRead helped readers better understand a research paper and its follow-on work compared to providing readers with a separate interface for faceted browsing of follow-on work.
items.why: Presents takeaway evaluation result for the CiteRead prototype.
items.plain: In a lab study, CiteRead helped readers understand a paper and its follow-on work better than using a separate browsing interface.

items.text: Usability studies of Scim have shown these highlights can reduce the time it takes readers to find specific information within a paper.
items.why: Presents takeaway evaluation result for the Scim prototype.
items.plain: User tests of Scim showed that its highlights help readers find specific information within a paper faster.

items.text: In a usability study, the above interactions reduced the time it took readers to find answers to questions involving the understanding of terminology.
items.why: Presents takeaway evaluation result for the ScholarPhi prototype.
items.plain: In a usability study, these features reduced the time readers spent looking for answers about terminology.

items.text: In a usability study, readers made more frequent use of passage summaries than definition tooltips when both were available, suggesting the potential value of plain language summaries as allowing readers to bypass definitions of individual terms when acquiring a broad understanding of a paper.
items.why: Presents takeaway evaluation result for the Paper Plain prototype.
items.plain: In a user study, readers used section summaries more often than term definitions, showing that simplified summaries help non-experts grasp a paper's main points without reading every definition.

items.text: A lab study showed that Threddy was able to lower the interaction costs of saving clips while maintaining context, allowed participants to curate research threads without breaking reading flows, and discover interesting new papers to further grow their understanding of the research fields.
items.why: Presents takeaway evaluation result for the Threddy prototype.
items.plain: A lab study showed that Threddy lowered the effort to save snippets while preserving context, allowing users to organize research topics while reading and discover new papers.

items.text: A usability study comparing Relatedly to a strong document-centric baseline showed that Relatedly led to participants writing summaries that were rated significantly more coherent, insightful, and detailed after 20 minutes of literature review.
items.why: Presents takeaway evaluation result for the Relatedly prototype.
items.plain: In a usability study, participants using Relatedly wrote summaries that were rated as significantly more coherent, insightful, and detailed after 20 minutes of review compared to a standard baseline.

items.text: The SciA11y system6 demonstrates this approach, automatically converting 12M academic PDFs to HTML [97]; a user study with blind and low vision participants demonstrated strong user appreciation of the output, though some errors remain (e.g., failing in certain cases to distinguish footnotes from body text, difficulty parsing math equations) [98].
items.why: Presents takeaway evaluation result for the SciA11y prototype.
items.plain: The SciA11y system automatically converted 12M academic PDFs to HTML, and a study with blind and low-vision participants showed strong user appreciation despite some remaining conversion errors.

items.text: This paper describes the Semantic Reader Project, which currently consists of ten research prototypes focusing on supporting scientists around Discovery [15, 82], Efficiency [28, 75], Comprehension [1, 33, 92], Synthesis [43, 73], and Accessibility [91, 97] when reading research papers.
items.why: Provides the overall summary of the ten prototypes across key themes.
items.plain: This paper presents the Semantic Reader Project, which includes ten prototypes supporting discovery, efficiency, comprehension, synthesis, and accessibility when reading research papers.

items.text: Validating our approach of augmenting existing PDFs of research papers, we have seen tremendous adoption of the freely-available Semantic Reader product1 which has grown to 10k weekly users.7 While we focused on augmenting PDF documents to support common scholar reading practices, all of our reading interfaces are built with web technologies—allowing these novel interactions to extend to future publication formats which can be rendered in web browsers.
items.why: Gives user metric and practical scope of the deployed reader.
items.plain: The freely available Semantic Reader tool has reached 10,000 weekly users, showing that enhancing existing PDF papers is a practical approach.
